title: Predict the output: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
keyPoints: double cannot represent 0.1 exactly in binary
Never use == for floating-point comparison – use Math.abs(a-b) < epsilon or BigDecimal
For money: always BigDecimal with String constructor
Understanding this concept is essential for Java interviews at senior level

s1_definition.oneliner: false. 0.1 + 0.2 in double is 0.30000000000000004, not exactly 0.3. IEEE 754 cannot represent 0.1 exactly in binary.
s1_definition.profdef:
The issue:

- `0.1` in binary is a repeating fraction (like 1/3 in decimal).
- `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004` due to floating-point rounding.
- `0.30000000000000004 == 0.3` is false.
s1_definition.analogy: Trying to express 1/3 exactly in decimal gives 0.333333... with rounding. Same issue: 0.1 in binary is a repeating fraction with rounding.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  0.1 in binary: 0.000110011001100110011... (repeating)
  0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 (rounding error)
  0.30000000000000004 == 0.3 → false

  Fix: Math.abs(a-b) < epsilon  or  BigDecimal
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false because IEEE 754 cannot represent 0.1 exactly in binary. Never use == for floating-point comparison. Use epsilon comparison or BigDecimal for exact money arithmetic.

One sentence to remember: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in double – use BigDecimal for money.
